newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU urged to focus more on booming Asian markets.
newsitem.headline: EU urged to focus more on booming Asian markets.

text.p: The European Union, which is lagging behind the competitive performance of trade rivals Japan and the United States, was urged on Wednesday to focus its trade and investments more on booming Asian markets.

"We have an embarrassingly small participation in fast growing Asia and that must be changed around," said Percy Barnevik, a leading European industrialist and chairman of an EU advisory group on how to improve Europe's competitive strength.

The advisory group, consisting of twelve European business, political and union leaders, presented a report showing that the 15-nation EU had been slipping in terms of both world trade and foreign direct investments since the 1970s.

European Commission President Jacques Santer will hand over the document, the group's fourth and last report in two years, to EU heads of state and government meeting in Dublin on Friday and Saturday.

It made several recommendations: trade between member states and the openness of the EU's single market must be improved, the EU should push for action to lift international barriers to trade, and Asian investments in Europe should be promoted.
The recommendations are directed at the European Commission, EU member states, institutions and companies.
Europe appeared well placed to take advantage of global integration because of its skilled labour force, entrepreneurial talent, exporting tradition and strong scientific research.
"Yet in spite of all this the EU has been losing ground in both the share of world trade and foreign direct investments," the report on "Europe's place in a globalising world economy" said.
It showed that the EU's share of world trade declined to 18 percent in 1992 from 24 percent in 1978 while Asia's share rose and the United States held on to its position.
"We are clearly losing ground," Barnevik said.

One reason for this poor performance was the EU's relatively small share of exports to South East Asia -- 11.9 percent of its total exports compared with 29.6 percent in Japan and 14.4 percent in the United States.
In contrast, the EU had a big market share in slower growing markets such as the Middle East and Africa.
Also, the share of the EU's external trade in relation to its gross domestic product has declined -- indicating diminishing global integration, the report said.
"Another reason is the product mix with too little in fast growing high tech exports and too much in medium and low tech sectors," the report added.
Reflecting this development, the EU has a widening trade deficit in net technology and and licences.
While the EU payment balance in those sectors went from zero in 1978 to a deficit of $11 billion in 1992, the surplus in the United States grew from $4 to $22 billion.
During the 1980s only Britain strengthened its comparative advantage in the high technology sector.
"We must move up the ladder, like Japan did after the war, like Korea is doing now," Barnevik said. "We must not shift away from high-tech sectors."

In the previous three reports the group made recommendations on the need to complete the single market and economic and monetary union. It also argued for greater investment in infrastructure and measures to boost integration between western and eastern Europe.
Parnevik, who has transformed Swiss-Swedish engineering giant ABB Asea Brown Boveri into one of the world's most respected firms, made clear that now was the time for action.
He said several measures were in the pipeline but that other proposals had not yet been acted upon.
"Execution now is everything," he said. "I don't think a lot of more bright ideas are required."
